concepts.def: Two-generation household of parents and dependent children; Parsons (1955) saw it as the ideal family of industrial society.
Three or more generations living together or in close contact; more common in pre-industrial and collectivist societies.
Step-family formed when separated adults remarry with children from prior relationships; around 11% of UK families with children (ONS).
Young and Willmott (1973): conjugal roles become more shared as families become privatised; criticised by Ann Oakley.
Murdock (1949): family performs four functions: sexual, reproductive, economic and educational.
Oakley (1974): housework remains gendered; women perform 'dual burden' of paid work and domestic labour.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Families — a core area of GCSE Sociology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Families brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Families.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between reliability and validity in research?
options: Reliability is whether a method produces consistent results when repeated; validity is whether it actually measures what it claims to. A method can be reliable but invalid, or valid but unreliable.
